sources.headline: Paraguay's former president charged after bank collapse
sources.text: Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.Peña, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal."Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent."It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".

sources.headline: Prosecutors Charge Paraguay’s Former President With Corruption
sources.text: Santiago Peña was impeached, removed from office, placed under house arrest and charged with using his office to enrich himself after a bank with close ties to his administration went under.

Paraguay: Senate impeached Peña rather than accept his offer to resign

Issued on: 08/11/2026 - 11:42

Paraguay's ousted president, Santiago Peña, has been charged over the collapse of Ueno Bank. Initially placed under house arrest, he has since been transferred to a military facility for his own safety. Nearly three million customers were locked out of their accounts after regulators seized control of the online bank. Repayments are now under way, but protests continue as customers demand access to their money. Peña denies any wrongdoing. Jack Pownall reports.

sources.headline: Ousted Paraguayan president appears before prosecutors
sources.text:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña waves after a meeting with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez at the Miraflores Presidential Palace in Caracas, on September 19, 2026.
Federico Parra/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
Federico Parra/AFP via Getty Images
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was impeached and placed under house arrest Friday after the collapse of a prominent U.S.-owned bank with ties to Paraguay's government. The fallout has left millions across the country without access to their money. Peña is one of Washington's closest allies in the region and was a shareholder in Ueno Bank, a digital lender that served about 3 million customers — more than half of the country's adult population. He was known as a pro-market leader focused on making it easier to do business in the country, but legislators said he jeopardized state assets and benefitted himself through his connection to the bank.
Ueno Bank previously said more than a million people opened bank accounts for the first time using its services, which included generous cash back offers on groceries.
A trial has proceeded against Peña, and he appeared before prosecutors Saturday morning. The last president ousted from office was Fernando Lugo in 2012. Peña has denied any wrongdoing but on Thursday he announced his resignation. Lawmakers refused to accept that resignation, and instead moved forward with the country's impeachment process. At proceedings inside the country's Senate Friday, legislators unanimously found Peña guilty of malfeasance in office, according to the Senate's website. Prosecutors then accused him of a breach of trust, among other charges, before placing him under house arrest. "I want to apologize to the Paraguayan people if I have failed you," Peña said in a speech posted to social media.
Demonstrators burn an image depicting Paraguay's President Santiago Pena, during a protest over the banking crisis and his resignation, at the main square in the surroundings of the National Congress in Asuncion, on November 5, 2026.
Daniel Duarte/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
Daniel Duarte/AFP via Getty Images
Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, was sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028. In a speech on Friday, he announced he would take action to compensate people whose money was lost in the bank's collapse. Paraguay's central bank said it seized control of Ueno Bank on Tuesday because its solvency ratio, an assessment of a company's long-term financial viability, no longer met legal standards.
Protests erupted across Asunción, the country's capital city, following the seizure. NPR's John Otis and Catherine Osborn contributed reporting to this story.

sources.headline: Paraguay's president under house arrest after bank collapse
sources.text:
November 7, 2026 / 5:12 AM EST
/ CBS/AP
Add CBS News on Google
Paraguay's president has been placed on house arrest on Friday after the collapse of a government-linked bank that locked nearly half the country's population out of their accounts.Paraguay's Senate voted to remove Santiago Peña for misconduct in office, making him the second president ousted by impeachment since the end of Gen. Alfredo Stroessner's 35-year dictatorship in 1989.Regulators had seized Ueno Bank just three days earlier, sending shock waves through the financial system and setting off the country's worst political crisis in more than a decade.
Santiago Pena, Paraguay's president, during a Bloomberg Television interview in New York, US, on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026.
Michael Nagle / Getty Images
Peña was ordered to remain at one of his homes in Asunción until he appears before prosecutors Saturday morning on charges of breach of trust, influence peddling and using public office for personal gain, the most serious of which carry up to 10 years in prison. Lawmakers accuse him of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.The Paraguayan president denied wrongdoing.When regulators seized the bank, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say they can't reach their money.
People queue outside a branch of the Banco Familiar hoping to be able to withdraw their savings or funds, a day after the intervention of the Ueno bank by Paraguay's Central Bank in Asuncion on November 4, 2026.
DANIEL DUARTE /Getty Images
The fallout has spread well beyond savers. A ride-hailing app that relied on Ueno shut down, leaving 3,000 drivers without work. The state power company says $21 million in loans from the Inter-American Development Bank and Taiwan, earmarked for public works, is trapped at the bank. Paraguay's bonds have posted some of the worst losses in emerging markets this week, and the guaraní has slid against the dollar.
Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaraníes (about $1,500). Deposits are insured up to about $35,000, which the central bank says covers 97% of Ueno's customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe.

sources.headline: Paraguay’s president quits after millions of people’s savings frozen in bank crisis
sources.text: Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days.At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers.Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers, leaving hundreds of thousands of families without access to money for food and basic daily expenses. Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests.In power since August 2023 and with a term running until 2028, the 47-year-old economist was already facing impeachment proceedings that had broad support.“Dear compatriots, today I address you at one of the most difficult moments of my life. With my heart set on Paraguay and with the conviction that our republic must always come before any person or circumstance, I have decided to submit my resignation as president of the republic,” said Peña in a video.Thousands of Paraguayans gathered outside Congress on Thursday to protest against Peña. Lawmakers voted unanimously on Thursday to launch impeachment proceedings against Peña over the crisis, alleging misconduct and a conflict of interest in dealings with the bank to which he is tied.Ueno Bank began as a finance company in the 1970s and, in 2021, was bought by Grupo Vázquez, one of Paraguay’s largest business and industrial conglomerates. At the end of 2023, it received authorisation from the central bank, already under Peña’s administration, to operate as a digital bank.The bank rapidly expanded its operations, attracting customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries and sponsoring Paraguay’s national football team. On Wednesday, the players released a letter “demanding” a “forceful response” from the government and the justice system.The bank came to manage between $800m and $850m in deposits from state and pension entities, including retirement funds, prompting criticism over conflicts of interest because of Peña’s previous shareholding ties to Ueno Holding.Peña said that, as an economist, he had merely made an “investment”, but that he had already disposed of all his shares. When the local press pointed to possible improper favouritism in directing state and pension funds to the bank, he called it a “false media campaign” aimed at weakening his government.On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers and even members of Peña’s Colorado party filed an impeachment motion holding the president responsible for the collapse. He had been a shareholder in the group that ran the bank until early last year and, in recent months, had reportedly been ignoring warnings from the central bank and the media about its operations.Political pressure intensified on Thursday morning when the ex-president Horacio Cartes, his former ally, posted a message endorsing the impeachment.“We will not stand on the side of the theft of public, private and pensioners’ funds. We must think of the people and of the values we uphold in the Colorado party. We support the impeachment of the president of the republic, Santiago Peña, in order to restore the institutional order of the republic,” he wrote.Other lawmakers followed suit and began debating impeachment when Peña released a video announcing his resignation.“I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions,” said the now former president.“I also want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed them … But today my priority is only one thing: the peace of mind of Paraguayans who trusted their savings to our financial system … My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he added.Since the scandal broke, Peña has insisted in interviews and statements that he committed no wrongdoing.Opposition senator Rafael Filizzola called the case “the biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era … This is a bank created from political power, to use public money for private businesses linked to political power, with the president of the republic at the head of it,” he told 1020 AM radio.Peña, a former finance minister who promised to rebuild a “great Paraguay”, was a key ally of the US president, Donald Trump, in the region – one of the few Latin American presidents to attend Trump’s second inauguration. US officials, including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, repeatedly praised him as a “strategic partner”, and Peña recently flew to Washington to discuss critical minerals and economic cooperation. Neither Rubio nor Trump has yet commented on Peña’s resignation.It is still unclear who will replace him or when, because his resignation must, in theory, be accepted by Congress – in which case the vice-president, Pedro Alliana, would take over. Alliana is also suspected of involvement in the Ueno Bank scandal, which he has denied.About an hour after Peña’s announcement, the lower house unanimously approved the impeachment motion, which now goes to the senate. If approved, even after his resignation, he would lose his senate seat and, with it, parliamentary immunity, leaving him to face any criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.

sources.headline: Paraguay President Pena resigns in wake of bank collapse
sources.text: Lawmakers are advancing impeachment proceedings against Pena, questioning his ties to the digital lender Ueno.Paraguay’s Congress has refused to accept President Santiago Pena’s resignation, pressing ahead with impeachment proceedings after the collapse of digital lender Ueno Bank.President since 2023, Pena had attempted to resign on Thursday as millions of Ueno customers remained unable to access their accounts.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3China sanctions Paraguay, Belize ministers over Taiwan tieslist 2 of 3Why are Latin American countries building closer ties with Israel?list 3 of 3Paraguay bank collapses with half of population’s savingsend of list“I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” the conservative politician said in a recorded address.But lawmakers declined to accept his resignation. The lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, and the Senate opened impeachment proceedings, summoning him to appear on Friday.A joint congressional session called to consider the resignation lost its quorum after lawmakers from Pena’s Colorado Party walked out, as it became clear there were not enough votes to accept it.Horacio Cartes, a leader in the Colorado Party, had posted a statement on social media indicating the group supported Pena’s impeachment.“We will not side with the theft of public, private and pension funds,” Cartes, a former president, wrote in his statement. “We must think of the people and the values we uphold in the Colorado Party.”Denying Pena’s resignation is likely to heighten the legal jeopardy he faces.Ordinarily, in Paraguay, presidents who leave office become senators for life, and they enjoy a degree of legal immunity from prosecution as members of the legislature.But that status is not conferred if the president is convicted in an impeachment trial.The political crisis erupted earlier this week, when Paraguay’s central bank announced that Ueno had fallen below the legal solvency ratio. Once its books were corrected, the bank’s capital – the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses – was less than half the legal minimum.Before its collapse, the company claimed it had about 3 million customers, in a country of 6.5 million people. Many have since lost access to their accounts and to pensions paid out through the bank.As part of a resolution to address the bank’s collapse, Paraguay’s central bank voted to transfer its remaining funds to other financial institutions.But the central bank itself came under scrutiny for not properly regulating Ueno. The central bank’s head, Carlos Carvallo, has since resigned.Pena himself formerly held a stake in Ueno’s parent company, Grupo Vazquez, though he said he sold those shares in 2025.Lawmakers, however, have accused Pena of having a conflict of interest and have questioned whether there was an institutional cover-up linked to the lender’s collapse.“He is accused of negligence at the very least and complicity in covering up the fact that the bank was insolvent,” said Al Jazeera’s Latin America editor Lucia Newman.“As I speak, there are people outside urging Congress not to accept the resignation of the president because they say that they want him tried and impeached.”Until its demise, Ueno had grown quickly from a niche company into a mid-tier bank administering close to $850m in public funds.Paraguay’s attorney general has also ordered three criminal investigations into the bank’s collapse, which will look into oversight of the lender and the placement of public funds in the institution. Pena has said he will cooperate with investigators.“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfil its purpose, and that public funds – as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans – be protected,” Pena added in his address.If Pena is ultimately removed from office, Vice President Pedro Alliana would likely take over as president.Ueno has made no public statement on the issue.

sources.headline: Paraguayan president resigns amid bank collapse leaving 3M people without access to bank accounts
sources.text:
Ousted Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest on Friday after he was impeached over a major banking crisis.
"He will remain under house arrest at his residence" in the capital, Asunción, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester told reporters.
She added that Peña would be questioned on Saturday over alleged crimes of breach of trust, influence peddling and misappropriation of funds following the collapse of Ueno Bank.
Peña had resigned on Thursday shortly before the Chamber of Deputies voted unanimously to impeach him.
Ueno Bank, which was placed under intervention earlier this week, had closed to three million customers, who suddenly found themselves without access to their accounts.
Protests have roiled the South American nation after its central bank took control of the Ueno on Tuesday, citing a severe capital shortfall.
Peña, a close ally of US President Donald Trump, announced his decision in a video posted to X as lawmakers debated his impeachment, saying he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."
"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed. It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," the right-wing president said in the video.
The ousted Paraguayan president, who until last year held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank, expressed regret but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the crisis, which has plunged a nation long prized by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil.
Some three million people lost access to bank accounts
Long lines of people trying to withdraw their money from Ueno branches snaked down Asuncion's streets on Tuesday and Wednesday, while angry protests swarmed the capital on both evenings.
Regulators investigating the bank found poorly documented lending and expenses wrongly accounted for as assets. But once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital fell half below the legal minimum, which led to the central bank seizing the lender.
Ueno’s app, cards and transfers went dark, and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks’ mobile apps, fueling public panic.
"In the face of these accusations, I can't pretend to be oblivious," said ruling party deputy Alejandro Aquilera during the debate. "We have more than three million Paraguayans who have been harmed, who feel betrayed, swindled, deceived," she said.
Ueno claimed 60% Paraguay's adults as customers
Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay’s adults as customers. They are now left scrambling to recoup their savings, government pensions, and, for 7,000 employees impacted by the bank's closure, unpaid wages.
Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno’s holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.
The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña’s long-ruling Colorado Party to the country’s regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.
“Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder.”
Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.
Ueno highly financed by Peña's government
Government money poured into Ueno’s coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.
As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million (€712 million) in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay’s giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees’ savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper.
Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million (€35 million) had gone to three such companies.
Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank’s oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

Published: 1:03am, 6 Nov 2026Updated: 7:35pm, 6 Nov 2026

Paraguayan President Santiago Pena is under criminal investigation following the collapse of a major digital bank, prosecutors have announced, as the South American leader prepares to defend himself before the Senate against possible removal from office on Friday.

The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Pena’s long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country’s most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration.

In a day of lightning-speed developments, Pena offered his resignation Thursday via social media, with the lower house voting unanimously to impeach him moments later. Both houses declined to accept Pena’s offer to resign, with the Senate instead deciding to press forward with a trial that could result in the president’s removal from office.

Opposition senators are continuing to demand that Pena be removed from office, arguing that allowing him to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution, should Paraguay’s Attorney General Emiliano Rolon Fernandez opt to file charges.

Rolon has ordered three criminal investigations into the Ueno Bank crisis, including allegations involving Pena and other current and former government officials, the prosecutor’s office said Thursday.

People hold signs during an anti-government protest in Asuncion, Paraguay, on Thursday. Photo: EPA

The investigations will examine authorities’ oversight of the bank, their handling of its failure and the placement of public funds in the lender.

Pena said he would cooperate with investigators. “Whatever the outcome of this process, I will act with responsibility and respect for the Constitution,” he said on X.

Earlier on Thursday, Pena said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of “the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions”.

Pena, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages.

If he is removed from office, Vice-President Pedro Alliana would replace him as Paraguay’s leader.

“I want to apologise to the people if I have failed them at any point,” he said. “It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me.”

Paraguay President Santiago Pena (left) and Vice-President Pedro Alliana attend their proclamation ceremony in Asuncion on May 30, 2023. Photo: AFP

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60 per cent of Paraguay’s adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Pena’s Colorado Party to the country’s regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings.

“Santiago Pena and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder.”

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cashback offers on groceries as it grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay’s national soccer team and plastered its name on the country’s main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno’s coffers under Pena. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly US$800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay’s giant hydroelectric dams.

But worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.

Crashing down

As recently as last month, Pena defended Ueno and the central bank’s oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno’s loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno’s capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank announced the lender’s seizure Tuesday, beginning a process to transfer deposits and recoverable assets to other banks before liquidating what remained.

Ueno’s app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks’ mobile apps, fuelling public panic.

Officials have appealed for calm.

A woman argues with Paraguayan police during a protest in Asuncion, Paraguay, on Wednesday. Photo: EPA

Under a law rushed through Congress on Wednesday, a state guarantee fund must repay stranded depositors within five business days, starting Thursday with small accounts of up to about US$1,600. The fund insures up to about US$36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97 per cent of clients.

On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, jailed pending trial and two others placed under house arrest. Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud.

Gustale’s lawyer pushed back on the charges, arguing that senior executives had relied on staff for lending decisions. “The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan,” Jose Fernandez Zacur told local media.

Still in their Ueno uniforms, young employees burned their credit cards and cursed Pena outside the Labour Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages. Pena’s resignation did little to calm them.

“Let the impeachment process take place and let him lose his immunity,” said Adolfo Villalba, one of the protesters on Thursday.

The Labour Ministry estimates the collapse has affected about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs at the bank and its related businesses.

Many saw Ueno’s collapse as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on Transparency International’s latest index of perceived corruption.

“This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labour,” said Belarmino Balbuena, one of thousands who marched on congress in the capital, Asuncion, on Wednesday.

sources.headline: Explainer-What is ueno bank and how did it trigger Paraguay's political crisis?
sources.text: Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena resigned on Nov 5 after the collapse of ueno, a prominent commercial bank with ties to his government.Here are more details on ueno and how its collapse led to the President’s downfall.What is ueno?Ueno, which spells its name with a lowercase “u”, is a digital lender that grew rapidly from a niche local fintech company into a mid-sized Paraguayan bank.Launched in 2021, ueno had been compared to other fast-growing digital banks like Nubank, Monzo or Revolut.As at June, the company said it had around 3 million customers – in a country of 6.5 million people – and administered roughly US$850 million (S$1.09 billion) in public funds, including money from state institutions and pension-related bodies.The bank’s rapid expansion made it one of Paraguay’s most visible financial success stories. But in recent months it came under regulatory scrutiny over alleged excessive lending to companies linked to its controlling shareholder, Grupo Vazquez.Paraguay’s central bank intervened after determining that ueno had breached minimum solvency requirements, triggering a crisis that left millions of customers temporarily unable to access their accounts.What links President Pena to ueno?Pena, an economist who was elected in 2023, has faced political scrutiny because of his past business ties to Grupo Vazquez. Pena has said he was a Grupo Vazquez shareholder until March 2025 when he sold his stake.Ueno says Pena never had a direct relationship with the bank as a shareholder or investor.Opposition lawmakers have accused Pena of conflict of interest, misuse of pension funds and institutional cover-up. Pena, who has repeatedly rejected any suggestion of improper ties, has described the controversy as the political escalation of what began as a regulatory issue and has argued that it should be addressed through the courts.Prosecutors said on Nov 5 that he was among those being investigated over the bank’s failure but he has not been taken in for questioning. They issued arrest warrants for eight ueno executives this week.How did regulators deal with ueno?Questions have focused on whether regulators adequately supervised ueno as it expanded, particularly because the country’s central bank chief, Carlos Carvallo, had previously been head of the digital lender.Carvallo resigned from the central bank on Nov 3 after it put ueno into resolution, its strongest measure short of immediate liquidation.The central bank has denied any conflict of interest, saying Carvallo recused himself from all decisions related to ueno.Nonetheless, pressure mounted after details of a regulatory probe became public, with lawmakers, banking industry representatives and opposition figures raising doubts as to whether there had been sufficient oversight.What has happened to the ueno accounts?The central bank said it was working to transfer ueno customer accounts to other financial institutions, a process that created strains across the banking system and contributed to outages at several banking apps.Customers are still unable to access their accounts within ueno. Some gathered outside ueno branches this week seeking access to their savings.Ueno’s mobile-first model helped attract new customers who were underserved by traditional banks and gave many Paraguayans easier access to digital payments, savings and other financial services.Those who have been unable to access their accounts include pensioners who receive state benefits through ueno, prompting the authorities to move quickly to guarantee deposits and safeguard public funds.Pena earlier this week approved legislation to help accelerate payments to depositors affected by the collapse of the bank.Could this affect Paraguay’s financial system more widely?The authorities say the crisis is limited to ueno and does not reflect broader weaknesses in Paraguay’s banking system.In addition to deposits, the bank said in a 2026 statement it had secured about US$510 million in financing from development institutions, international funds and capital markets. These include a US$350 million bond issuance on Wall Street led by JPMorgan and Bank of America.Paraguay has won investment-grade credit ratings and built a reputation as one of South America’s more stable and reform-friendly economies. It is unclear if the crisis will affect the country’s reputation in the longer term. REUTERS
